For fixed objective coefficients a_t and independently sampled, unbiased task gradients with covariance Σ_t, separately normalized task means give Cov(g)=Σ_t a_t²Σ_t/n_t for deterministic positive counts. By total covariance, random counts replace 1/n_t with E[1/N_t]; conditional on nonempty tasks, Jensen implies a variance penalty relative to fixed counts at the same mean. Negative correlation between complementary task counts does not itself create cross-task gradient covariance: conditional means remain constant. Shared examples/randomness can create cross-covariance. Zero-count tasks require explicit handling; skipping them generally changes the expected objective. Bernoulli selection with inverse-probability weighting instead adds task-selection noise involving gradient means. These are direct estimator calculations consistent with [stratified-SGD theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3080).

Minimizing covariance trace at fixed total examples yields Neyman allocation n_t ∝ |a_t|√tr(Σ_t); with per-example costs c_t and fixed compute, n_t ∝ |a_t|√[tr(Σ_t)/c_t]. Assumptions: independent sampling, finite variances, unbiased gradients for the intended normalization, and locally representative variance/cost estimates. This optimizes a scalar variance criterion, not every covariance direction. For variable supervised-token counts K, distinguish averaging example means from pooling tokens. The latter is a ratio estimator: with example gradient sum S and μ=E[S]/E[K], its approximate covariance is Cov(S−μK)/(nE[K]²), incorporating within-example token dependence and finite-batch ratio bias. See [ratio-estimator linearization](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/sampling/html/vartaylor_ratio.html).

Lower gradient variance alone guarantees neither faster Adam convergence nor better validation performance: allocation also changes Adam’s adaptive second moments. Guarantees require specific smoothness, noise, and optimizer assumptions; vanilla Adam has convergence counterexamples ([Reddi et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09237)). A frozen-preconditioner allocation can use tr(PΣ_tPᵀ), but remains a local approximation. No universal theory justifies p=0.75 without measured task variances, coefficients, costs, and normalization.
